sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.17072", "title": "Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation", "abstract": "Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.10866", "title": "The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training", "abstract": "How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.13276", "title": "An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines", "abstract": "Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.07598", "title": "Align Before Aggregation: Basis-Consistent Federated LoRA under Heterogeneous Ranks", "abstract": "Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) under heterogeneous client capacities is increasingly important, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with heterogeneous ranks makes it practical. Existing server-side aggregators compose local matrix updates $ΔW_i$ from client-specific LoRA factors $(A_i,B_i)$ before aggregating them. Although these matrix updates lie in the same weight space $\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times n}$ and can be averaged directly, the LoRA factors that generate them may expressed client-specific local basis. In the typical compose--aggregate--factorize--dispatch loop, this basis inconsistency can make the rank-$r_i$ reference prefix dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after server-side refactorization. In this work, we propose \\textbf{FedAbA}, a basis-consistent federated LoRA aggregation framework for heterogeneous ranks. FedAbA first extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, and constructs a basis-consistent reconstruction of each local matrix update before aggregation. It then aggregates these reconstructions with weights that combine client data size and consistency score, followed by exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch. Our theoretical analysis clarifies the role of basis consistency and supports the proposed consistency-aware aggregation mechanism. Extensive experiments show that FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.11537", "title": "Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer", "abstract": "Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) optimize circuit angles through repeated quantum-device evaluations, often facing vanishing gradients and high optimization costs. We ask whether a large language model (LLM) can write these angles directly. Extending *weight-space programming* from classical networks to quantum circuits, we provide a frontier LLM (\\gpt) with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions. Its angles are executed exactly as written, without returning losses, gradients, or accuracy feedback. Across 139 requests, we test handwritten-digit classification, VQE ground-state estimation for spin chains and H$_2$, and MaxCut QAOA, comparing against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit. When parameters have interpretable structure, the LLM matches or approaches the optimizer: it achieves 95--100\\% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H$_2$ ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93--96\\% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12--18 hand-written weights, outperforming an optimizer trained on the same ten examples. Its weights are also strong warm starts: optimization reaches its best value after a median of one evaluation rather than hundreds. Allowed to design circuits, the LLM chooses data-dependent rotation chains encoding pixel importance in all 30 cases (one qubit for binary tasks, one chain per qubit for ten classes), reaching 65\\% accuracy across ten digits. Yet the approach fails in opaque weight spaces: accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, while optimization improves. It is also sensitive to gate conventions: 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail. We release all prompts, replies, and scores.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.11902", "title": "Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models", "abstract": "Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.07610", "title": "Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone", "abstract": "When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.20288", "title": "Protecting Safety during Reasoning Training with Low-Rank Fisher Regularisation", "abstract": "Large language models are trained to have safety guardrails, but these can be compromised while fine-tuning for new capabilities, such as reasoning. One way to mitigate this degradation is to modify the fine-tuning objective to preserve safety behaviour, but doing so effectively and efficiently remains challenging. We revisit Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which penalises parameter updates based on sensitivity estimates from the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). While EWC provides some protection, the diagonal approximation ignores interactions between parameters. We address this limitation by exploiting recent findings that safety-relevant behaviour is located in a low-rank subspace within models. Our method, Subspace-Projected Elastic Weight Consolidation (SP-EWC), projects gradients onto this subspace to capture non-diagonal curvature efficiently. We investigate three different ways of identifying the safety subspace: through safety fine-tuning updates (LoRA), safety-related activations (ActSVD), and contrastive representations of safety and utility data (cPCA). We find that this choice substantially affects performance, with SP-EWC using cPCA comparing favourably against existing methods by better maintaining safety guardrails without introducing excessive over-refusal.", "abstract_truncated": false}, {"paper_id": "2611.19382", "title": "Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity", "abstract": "Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \\emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.", "abstract_truncated": false}]}

to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. At this scale, existing fine-tuning and meta-learning methods still estimate target-specific updates from extremely sparse feedback, leaving the update direction weakly identified. decision.question: Compared with AdamW, GaLore, and LDAdam, what are ResQAdam's measured peak GPU training memory, model-quality results, and throughput across model sizes and QAT settings?

result.question: Compared with AdamW, GaLore, and LDAdam, what are ResQAdam's measured peak GPU training memory, model-quality results, and throughput across model sizes and QAT settings?

passages.text: Motivated by this insight, we propose ResQAdam ( Res idual-Preserving Q uantization-Aware Adam ), a geometrically decoupled optimizer that applies distinct update rules based on subspace characteristics. It stores one dense momentum in BF16 and refreshes its top- r r singular vectors every τ \tau steps. Adam runs on the r × r r\times r coordinates of the gradient in this subspace, and the residual of the momentum contributes a sign update whose norm matches the Adam update. Since no dense second moment is kept, persistent optimizer memory falls to roughly a quarter of AdamW, and the SVD cost is spread over τ \tau steps. By eliminating dense second-moment tracking, ResQAdam limits the persistent optimizer memory footprint to only the BF16 momentum and negligible low-rank components. For a weight matrix W ∈ ℝ n × m W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} with projection rank r r , the persistent memory ratio compared to standard AdamW is: 2 ​ n ​ m + 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( n + m ) ​ r + r 2 ) / 8 ​ n ​ m ≈ 25 % 2nm+\mathcal{O}((n+m)r+r^{2})/{8nm}\approx 25\% . The measured saving is 71% to 74%. Furthermore, while the required SVD introduces computational overhead, refreshing the bases only once every few hundred steps effectively amortizes this cost, resulting in minimal training-speed degradation.

To evaluate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments across both from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning paradigms. Across multiple LLM architectures, quantization configurations, and QAT methods, our empirical results demonstrate that ResQAdam closely tracks the optimization trajectory and largely preserves AdamW-level final performance across the evaluated settings. It achieves this by reducing around 75% of AdamW’s average memory footprint, while introducing negligible computational overhead for training.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 2 compares ResQAdam with AdamW across the three fine-tuning recipes, which differ in data source, training objective and optimization granularity. Across these settings, ResQAdam generally achieves performance close to AdamW in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, while reducing optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74%. Although some aggressive W2A16 block-wise settings show larger metric fluctuations, the overall results indicate that ResQAdam can serve as a memory-efficient alternative to AdamW for diverse QAT fine-tuning pipelines.

Table 3: Comparison of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput across different models. Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA; Hu et al., 2022 ) is a standard parameter-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning: it scales to large models, is easy to compose with existing training stacks, and is widely treated as the default way to specialize a pretrained language model on a new task or domain Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) ; Biderman et al. (2024) . A common piece of practitioner wisdom is that increasing LoRA rank increases adapter capacity: a larger r r enlarges the low-rank update subspace and can support richer task-specific changes Raschka (2023) ; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) ; Liu et al. (2024b) . This intuition is appealing and often borne out at moderate ranks, yet it rests on an implicit assumption that is rarely checked: that the adapter actually uses the subspace it is given.

In parallel, fine-tuning, whether full-rank or parameter-efficient, faces a persistent learning–forgetting tension. Fitting a target distribution can improve task metrics while erasing competence on broad pretraining domains, and heterogeneous or sequential training regimes exacerbate the trade-off Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) ; Hu et al. (2022) . LoRA is not exempt: in mixed-domain and continual-learning settings, adapters often lag full fine-tuning on target-task fit while still paying a substantial retention cost on pretraining proxies Biderman et al. (2024) ; Shuttleworth et al. (2024) . Prior work has proposed many remedies, such as stronger parameterizations Kopiczko et al. (2024) , norm constraints Wang et al. (2025) , spectral initialization Meng et al. (2025) , and deliberately tiny adapters Morris et al. (2026) . However, these approaches frequently reallocate the trade-off rather than improve it: methods that fit the fine-tuning mixture well can forget aggressively, whereas methods that limit forgetting often underfit the new data (Figure 2 ).

Our primary supervised fine-tuning (SFT) experiments fine-tune Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B with assistant-only loss; adaptation is restricted to the MLP down-projection matrices. LoRA-based methods use the maximum feasible rank for this policy on the base model ( r = 896 r{=}896 ), with scaling α = 2 ​ r \alpha{=}2r . Dense down-projection fine-tuning updates the same dense down_proj subset rather than the entire checkpoint. Comparisons across adapter parameterizations are based on each method’s published or default hyperparameters and are not parameter-count matched; trainable parameter totals are reported in Table 5 .

Low-capacity baselines (VeRA, TinyLoRA, SVF) occupy a different parameter budget than rank- 896 896 LoRA and should be read as an underfitting regime rather than a matched-capacity head-to-head. PiSSA and SVF differ from standard LoRA in how scaling constants enter the forward pass. We record the trainable parameter count for every configuration.

selections.summary: Defines behavioral rate as the serialized adapter size needed to retain a specified share of held-out fine-tuning gain. Reports that LoRA compressibility varies across frozen base models and that data-measured correction spectra rank rates within a base model.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses whether low-rank compression preserves acquired behavior, rather than merely reconstructing weights.

evidence.quote: the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain
fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone

selections.summary: Proposes an SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer for LoRA. In reported mixed-domain sweeps, it improves mean Wiki perplexity against unpenalized LoRA at tested ranks of at least 16.
selections.relevance: Direct match for spectral regularization, effective rank, and language-model fine-tuning. Cross-method comparisons are not parameter-count matched.

evidence.quote: our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss.
Comparisons across adapter parameterizations are based on each method’s published or default hyperparameters and are not parameter-count matched

evidence.quote: the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training

leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion

evidence.quote: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy

In the reported hardware comparison, optimizer-state memory falls by 71.3%–73.2%, total peak memory by 15.3%–19.5%, and throughput by 0.6%–1.4% versus AdamW.

All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096.

selections.relevance: Covers the profile’s communication, throughput, and model-quality tradeoffs beyond low-rank methods.

evidence.quote: Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56$\times$ end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.
